name: Martin Luther King Jr.
info: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was an American Baptist minister and civil rights leader who led the Montgomery bus boycott, headed the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and used nonviolent protest against segregation until his assassination in Memphis.

facts.born: 15 January 1929 in Atlanta, Georgia, as Michael King Jr.; second of three children of the Baptist minister Michael King and Alberta King (née Williams); his name was changed in 1934 to Martin Luther King Jr.
facts.died: 4 April 1968 in Memphis, Tennessee; shot by James Earl Ray at the Lorraine Motel at 6:01 p.m. and pronounced dead at St. Joseph's Hospital at 7:05 p.m.; his remains were moved in 1977 to a tomb at what is now the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park
facts.role: Baptist minister; pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery (from 1954); leader of the Montgomery bus boycott (1955–1956); first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (1957–1968); co-pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, Atlanta (from 1960)
facts.known: the Montgomery bus boycott; nonviolent protest against Jim Crow laws; the Birmingham campaign and the Letter from Birmingham Jail; the 1963 March on Washington and the I Have a Dream speech; the Selma voting rights marches; the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize; opposition to the Vietnam War and the Poor People's Campaign

t: A Baptist minister's son from Atlanta, King became the best-known spokesman of the civil rights movement after leading the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted 385 days and ended with a ruling against segregated buses.

Through the Southern Christian Leadership Conference he led nonviolent campaigns at Birmingham, in Selma and elsewhere, and the movement won legislative gains in the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

In his last years he opposed the Vietnam War and poverty, lost allies for doing so, was surveilled by the FBI, and was shot dead in Memphis on 4 April 1968 while supporting striking sanitation workers.
dyk: King was born Michael King Jr. In 1934, after a trip that took his father to Berlin and to sites in Germany linked to the Reformation leader Martin Luther, the father changed his own name, and his five-year-old son's, to Martin Luther King.
ev: Born in Atlanta, Georgia, the second of three children of a Baptist minister and his wife
Graduates from Morehouse College with a Bachelor of Arts in sociology, aged nineteen
Receives his PhD from Boston University and leads the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasts 385 days
Helps found the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and becomes its first president
Writes the Letter from Birmingham Jail and delivers the I Have a Dream speech at the March on Washington
Becomes the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize; the Civil Rights Act is passed
Leads marchers to the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma and speaks at the end of the march to Montgomery
Shot at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis on 4 April and dies the same evening

sections.early:
Martin Luther King Jr. was born Michael King Jr. on 15 January 1929 in Atlanta, the second of three children of Michael King and Alberta King (née Williams). His maternal grandfather, Adam Daniel Williams, had become pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church in 1894, and King Sr. took the pulpit in 1931. In 1934 the church sent King Sr. on a trip that included Berlin and sites in Germany associated with Martin Luther; he then changed his own name and his son's. The family lived on the second floor of the grandparents' home until 1941.

King began at Yonge Street Elementary School, a school for black children, in September 1935, and soon afterwards the parents of a white playmate stopped allowing the boys to play together. His parents spoke to him of the history of slavery and racism, which King later said made him "determined to hate every white person", and told him it was his Christian duty to love everyone. He saw his father refuse to accept segregation in a shoe store and lead a march to Atlanta's city hall in 1936 over voting rights discrimination.

In April 1944 he won an oratorical contest, and on the bus home he and his teacher were ordered to stand for white passengers. King wrote that it was "the angriest I have ever been in my life". In 1944, aged 15, he passed the entrance examination for Morehouse College. In 1947 he chose the ministry, crediting the college's president, Benjamin Mays, as his "spiritual mentor", and in 1948 he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in sociology.
sections.rise:
King studied at Crozer Theological Seminary in Upland, Pennsylvania, where he was elected president of the student body, and graduated with a Bachelor of Divinity in 1951. He then began doctoral studies in systematic theology at Boston University. He met Coretta Scott there, and they married on 18 June 1953; they had four children, Yolanda, Martin Luther King III, Dexter Scott and Bernice. In 1954, at the age of 25, he was called as pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama, and he received his PhD on 5 June 1955.

In March 1955 a schoolgirl, Claudette Colvin, refused to give up her bus seat to a white man in Montgomery, and on 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks was arrested for the same refusal. The Montgomery bus boycott that followed was urged and planned by Edgar Nixon and led by King, whom the other ministers asked to take the role because his newness to community leadership made it easier for him to speak out. It lasted 385 days. His house was bombed, and he was arrested for travelling 30 mph in a 25 mph zone, which drew national media attention. It ended when a US District Court ruling in Browder v. Gayle prohibited segregation on Montgomery's buses.

In 1957 King, with Ralph Abernathy, Fred Shuttlesworth, Joseph Lowery, Bayard Rustin and others, founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), and he led it until his death. In September 1958 he was stabbed in the chest with a letter opener by Izola Curry, who was later found mentally incompetent to stand trial. In February and March 1959 he travelled to India, a journey that deepened his understanding of nonviolent resistance.
sections.deeds:
After the failed Albany Movement of 1961–1962 in Georgia, where, after nearly a year of activism with few tangible results, the movement declined and the national media criticised his role, King chose engagements the SCLC could control. In April 1963 the SCLC began a campaign against segregation and economic injustice in Birmingham, Alabama. Its tactics were nonviolent but intentionally confrontational, and King's aim was to provoke mass arrests and "create a situation so crisis-packed that it will inevitably open the door to negotiation." Police under Eugene "Bull" Connor used high-pressure water jets and dogs against protesters, children among them, and television footage shocked many white Americans. Connor lost his job and the "Jim Crow" signs came down. Jailed during the campaign, King wrote the Letter from Birmingham Jail, which argued that "freedom is never voluntarily given by the oppressor; it must be demanded by the oppressed."

On 28 August 1963 King was one of the leaders of the "Big Six" organisations behind the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, attended by more than a quarter of a million people. There he delivered a 17-minute speech later known as "I Have a Dream". In October 1964 he became the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize.

In Selma, Alabama, the SCLC joined the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee in a voting rights campaign. After the violence of Bloody Sunday on 7 March 1965, at which King was not present, he led marchers to the Edmund Pettus Bridge on 9 March, and the march to Montgomery was completed on 25 March. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 enacted most of the rights the movement had demanded.
sections.opponents:
FBI director J. Edgar Hoover treated King as a radical and made him a target of COINTELPRO. The FBI wiretapped him from the fall of 1963 under an authorisation from Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, which Hoover treated as wider than Kennedy had written it, and investigated claims of communist ties. By 1976 the FBI had acknowledged that it had found no evidence that King or the SCLC were involved with communist organisations. King denied any such connection. In 1975 the Church Committee found that King had been the target of "an intensive campaign" by the FBI to "neutralize" him. Just before the Nobel Prize the FBI sent him an anonymous letter with a tape of wiretapped recordings; King took it as an attempt to drive him to suicide, while William Sullivan argued it may have been meant to make him resign from the SCLC.

Critics within the movement also challenged him. Malcolm X called the March on Washington the "Farce on Washington", and Ella Baker regarded King as a media figure who had lost touch with the grassroots. Stokely Carmichael rejected King's plea for integration and thought America had no conscience to appeal to. After Birmingham, King and the SCLC were criticised for putting children in harm's way. Rustin resigned from the Poor People's Campaign, calling its demands unrealisable.

King's speech against the Vietnam War, "Beyond Vietnam", of April 1967, cost him white allies including President Johnson and Billy Graham. Life magazine called it "demagogic slander", and The Washington Post said he had "diminished his usefulness to his cause, his country, his people." In 1991 an inquiry at Boston University concluded that portions of his doctoral dissertation were plagiarised, but advised against revoking the degree.
sections.last:
In his last years King widened his aims to poverty and the war. In 1968 he and the SCLC organised the Poor People's Campaign, intended to gather "a multiracial army of the poor" in Washington to press for an "economic bill of rights". On 29 March 1968 he went to Memphis, Tennessee, to support black sanitation workers on strike since 12 March. On 3 April he gave the "I've Been to the Mountaintop" address at Mason Temple.

King was shot by James Earl Ray at 6:01 p.m. on 4 April 1968 as he stood on the second-floor balcony of the Lorraine Motel, and he died at St. Joseph's Hospital at 7:05 p.m. The assassination led to riots in Washington, Chicago, Baltimore, Louisville, Kansas City and dozens of other cities, and Johnson declared 7 April a national day of mourning. Memphis settled the strike on terms favourable to the workers. The Poor People's Campaign went ahead, and demonstrators on the National Mall stayed six weeks in a camp called "Resurrection City".

Ray was captured at London Heathrow Airport two months later. He confessed on 10 March 1969, recanted three days later, and, on his lawyer's advice, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 99 years. He claimed that a man called "Raoul" was involved. In 1999 a jury in a civil suit brought by the King family found Loyd Jowers and "other unknown co-conspirators" liable, but in 2000 the Department of Justice found no evidence of conspiracy. King researchers David Garrow and Gerald Posner disagreed with William F. Pepper's claim that the government killed King, while Jesse Jackson said he would never believe that Ray acted alone.
sections.legacy:
Within days of King's death Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1968, whose Title VIII, the Fair Housing Act, prohibited discrimination in housing; it was seen as a tribute to his struggle against residential discrimination. In 1968 Coretta Scott King founded the King Center in Atlanta. Cities and states began holidays for King in 1971, President Ronald Reagan signed a bill for a federal holiday on 2 November 1983, and Martin Luther King Jr. Day was first observed on 20 January 1986. Jimmy Carter awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1977, calling him "the conscience of his generation", and Congress awarded the Congressional Gold Medal in 2003. A memorial to him was dedicated in 2011 on the National Mall.

His thinking was shaped by the Sermon on the Mount, by Gandhi, Thoreau, Walter Rauschenbusch, Reinhold Niebuhr and Paul Tillich. Late in life he said that America needed a "radical revolution of values" and spoke of the "giant triplets of racism, materialism and militarism". He rejected communism and also laissez-faire capitalism, and in private sometimes spoke of support for democratic socialism.

His influence reached beyond the United States. Albert Luthuli of South Africa cited his work, and John Hume cited King's legacy in the Northern Ireland civil rights movement. Native American leaders such as John Echohawk of the Native American Rights Fund said they were inspired by him. The Episcopal Church and the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America commemorate him liturgically, and in 2016 Archbishop Timothy Paul of the Holy Christian Orthodox Church canonised him.

summary: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968), a Baptist minister from Atlanta, led the Montgomery bus boycott and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, and used nonviolent protest against segregation in Birmingham, Selma and elsewhere. He won the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize, opposed the Vietnam War and poverty, and was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

notes: Birth name and year: the article gives Michael King Jr., 15 January 1929; the name change in 1934 is as the article gives it (the father changed both names after returning in August 1934).
Albany: the article says King's first visit was in December 1961 and that he returned in July 1962; the section gives only the article's summary that the movement declined after nearly a year.

Bloody Sunday: the article says King was not present; the text 'at which King was not present' follows it. The article also says 'On March 5' King met Johnson administration officials, which does not fit its sequence; left out.

Conspiracy: the article reports the 1999 civil jury finding that Jowers was complicit and that government agencies were party to the assassination; only the Jowers part and the 2000 Department of Justice finding are given, with the sister's retraction left out for space.

Left out: the 1950 Mary's Cafe sit-in (its significance as the first use of nonviolence is the article's 'believed' claim and rests on one local researcher), the 2019 FBI file allegation (the article says historians dismiss it as unreliable), the allegations of extramarital affairs (the article gives them as FBI claims and as Garrow's and Abernathy's differing accounts; the text states only the FBI tape), King's relationship with Betty Moitz, the Scripto strike, Chicago 1966, St. Augustine, Atlanta sit-ins and the Reagan-era holiday details beyond the signing and first observance.
Rankings and polls (Gallup, Time, Discovery Channel), the five-dollar bill, Star Trek, Grammy and honorary degrees were left out as the guide asks.
The article gives King's Nobel Prize date as 14 October 1964 (the announcement); the text says only 1964.
Section 'rise' follows the article's order of 1954 pastorate and 5 June 1955 PhD; the Boston University dissertation inquiry is placed under opponents.
